title: Measuring a rise or a fall
objectives: Compute a percentage change from the original value, not the new one
Measure rises and falls, including rises over 100%
Compute a daily return from two closing prices

screens.title: Measuring a rise or a fall
screens.prose: A price moves from one value to another. We want one number for the size of the move, as a percentage. The question is: a percentage of which price?
A share closed at £40.00 on Monday. By Friday its price had risen by 25%.
screens.question: Set Friday's bar to Friday's closing price.

hints.text: What is 25% of £40.00? Think of a quarter.
Monday's bar is the price the 25% is measured against.
A quarter of £40.00 is £10.00. Friday's price is £40.00 plus £10.00.

feedback.correct: A rise of £10.00 on £40.00 takes the price to £50.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find 25% of Monday's price, then add it on.

byKey.added-pounds: You added £25.00. The rise is 25% of £40.00, which is £10.00.
byKey.rise-only: You set the bar to the rise itself. Friday's price is Monday's £40.00 plus the £10.00 rise.

explain.text: 25% of £40.00 is £10.00, so Friday's close is £50.00. In one step that is $40 \times 1.25 = 50$. The 25% was measured against Monday's price, where the move started.

screens.prose: A different week. The share starts again at £40.00 on Monday. By Wednesday it has fallen by 25%.
screens.question: Drag the Wednesday point to Wednesday's price.

hints.text: A fall of 25% of £40.00 is how many pounds?
Start from Monday's price and move left.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find 25% of £40.00 and move that far left.

byKey.fall-size: You placed the size of the fall, £10.00. The price is what is left after it: £30.00.
byKey.wrong-way: You moved the price up. A fall moves it left, to a lower price.
byKey.pounds: You took £25.00 off. The fall is 25% of £40.00, which is £10.00.

explain.text: The fall is £10.00, so Wednesday's price is £30.00. That is $40 \times 0.75 = 30$: a 25% fall keeps 75% of the price. Again the 25% was measured from Monday, the starting price.

screens.prose: Now turn it round. You know both prices and want the percentage. The share went from £40.00 on Monday to £46.00 on Friday.
screens.question: By what percentage did the price rise?

hints.text: The rise is £6.00. What fraction of the starting price is that?
Measure the rise against Monday's bar.
$\dfrac{6}{40} = 0.15$. Write that as a percentage.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the rise by Monday's price.

byKey.pounds: You gave the rise in pounds. The question asks what percentage of £40.00 the £6.00 is.
byKey.new-base: You divided by £46.00, the new price. The rise is measured from where it started, £40.00.
byKey.ratio: That is Friday's price as a percentage of Monday's. Take away the 100% you started with.

explain.text: You divided the £6.00 rise by the £40.00 start: $\tfrac{6}{40} = 0.15$, a 15% rise. The price a change is measured from is the **original** value. Check: $40 \times 1.15 = 46$.

screens.prose: Now a fall. The share closed at £80.00 on Monday and at £68.00 on Friday.
screens.question: By what percentage did the price fall?

hints.text: How many pounds did the price fall?
The original price is Monday's.

feedback.correct: A £12.00 fall on £80.00 is a 15% fall.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the fall by Monday's price.

byKey.pounds: You gave the fall in pounds. As a share of the £80.00 start it is 15%.
byKey.new-base: You divided by £68.00, the new price. Divide by £80.00, where the fall started.

explain.text: The fall is £12.00 and the original is £80.00: $\tfrac{12}{80} = 0.15$. A fall works the same way as a rise: change over original. Check: $80 \times 0.85 = 68$.

screens.prose: A small company's share jumps from £12.00 to £30.00 after good news.
screens.question: By what percentage did the price rise?

hints.text: The rise is £18.00. Compare it with £12.00.
Is the rise bigger or smaller than the original price?

feedback.correct: The £18.00 rise is one and a half times the original £12.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the rise by the price before the jump.

byKey.ratio: 250% is the new price as a percentage of the old. The rise is that minus 100%.
byKey.pounds: You gave the rise in pounds. Divide the £18.00 by the £12.00 original.
byKey.new-base: You divided by £30.00, the new price. Divide by £12.00, where the jump started.

explain.text: The rise is bigger than the original, so the percentage is over 100%: $\tfrac{18}{12} = 1.5$, a 150% rise. A fall can never pass 100%, because a price cannot drop below £0.00.

screens.prose: A share falls from £50.00 to £40.00. Sam says: the fall is £10.00, and £10.00 is 25% of £40.00, so it fell 25%.
screens.question: What is the percentage fall?

options.why: You divided by £40.00, the price after the fall, as Sam did. The fall is measured from £50.00.
You wrote the £10.00 fall as 10%. As a share of £50.00 it is a fifth.
80% is the new price as a share of the old. The fall is the part that went: 100% minus 80%.

hints.text: Where did the fall start?
The original is the price before the fall.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the fall by the price it fell from.

byKey.sam: You divided by the new price, £40.00, as Sam did. A change is always measured from the original, £50.00.

explain.text: Sam divided by the new price. The fall started at £50.00, so it is $\tfrac{10}{50} = 0.2$, a 20% fall. Going back up from £40.00 to £50.00 would be a 25% rise: the same £10.00, a different original.

screens.prose: Every time, you found the change and divided by the original value: $$\text{percentage change} = \dfrac{\text{new} - \text{original}}{\text{original}} \times 100\%$$ A negative answer is a fall.
screens.question: A price goes from £25.00 to £27.00. Which calculation gives the percentage change?

options.why: You divided by the new price. The original, £25.00, goes on the bottom.
That is the new price as a multiple of the old. Take away 1 to leave the change.
That is the change in pounds. It still needs dividing by the original.

hints.text: Which price did you divide by on every screen?

feedback.correct: The change over the original: $\tfrac{2}{25} = 0.08$, an 8% rise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the change on top and the original underneath.

explain.text: On every screen the bottom of the fraction was the price before the move. Here that is £25.00: $\tfrac{27 - 25}{25} = 0.08$, an 8% rise.

screens.prose: We can reach the same rule from multipliers. A change is one multiplication, $\text{new} = \text{original} \times m$. Build the rule from that.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\text{new} = \text{original} \times m$, a change is one multiplication
$m = \dfrac{\text{new}}{\text{original}}$, divide both sides by the original
$m - 1 = \dfrac{46 - 40}{40} = 0.15$, check with Monday and Friday: a 15% rise

hints.text: Which line is where every change starts?
You need $m$ on its own before you can take 1 from it.
Start from new = original × m. Divide by the original to get $m$. Then take 1 away, then check.

feedback.correct: Dividing by the original is what puts it on the bottom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the multiplication, then get $m$ on its own.

byKey.l3: Taking 1 away needs $m$ on its own first. Find $m$ before this line.
byKey.l4: The check uses the finished rule, so it comes last.

explain.text: Dividing by the original put it on the bottom, which is why every screen divided by the starting price. Taking 1 away removes the 100% you started with. So $m - 1$ is the percentage change as a decimal.

screens.prose: A stock's **daily return** is the percentage change from yesterday's close to today's. The chart shows five daily closing prices.
screens.question: What is the return from day 3 to day 4? Give a percentage.

hints.text: Which close is the original here?
Yesterday's close, £82.50, is the original.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the change by yesterday's close.

byKey.pounds: You gave the change in pounds. Divide it by yesterday's £82.50 close.
byKey.new-base: You divided by today's close, £84.15. A return is measured from yesterday's close.

explain.text: Yesterday's close is the original: $\tfrac{84.15 - 82.50}{82.50} = 0.02$, a 2.00% return. A test of a strategy on past prices repeats this for every day. Dividing by today's price instead would put a small error into every return.

ideas: A percentage change compares the change with the original value, the one the move started from.
Rises and falls work the same way: change over original, then written as a percentage.
A rise can be more than 100%. A fall cannot, because a price cannot drop below zero.

formula.name: Percentage change
formula.note: A negative answer is a fall.

summary.trap: Dividing by the new price. From £50.00 to £40.00 is a 20% fall, not 25%.

options.why: You divided the £15.00 rise by £75.00, the new price. Divide by £60.00.
You wrote the £15.00 rise as a percentage. Divide it by £60.00 first.
That is the new price as a percentage of the old. The rise is 125% minus 100%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the rise by the original price.

explain.text: The rise is £15.00 and the original is £60.00: $\tfrac{15}{60} = 0.25$, a 25% rise.

feedback.correct: An 80p fall on £3.20 is a quarter.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the fall by the price before it.

byKey.new-base: You divided by £2.40, the new price. Divide the 80p fall by £3.20.
byKey.kept: 75% is what is left of the price. The fall is the 25% that went.

explain.text: The fall is £0.80 and the original is £3.20: $\tfrac{0.8}{3.2} = 0.25$, a 25% fall.

quiz.prose: Share A rises from £8.00 to £10.00. Share B rises from £100.00 to £120.00.
quiz.question: Which had the bigger percentage rise?

options.why: You compared the pound rises, £2.00 and £20.00. As a share of each original, A rose 25% and B rose 20%.

options.text: They rose by the same percentage
options.why: You expected two rises that look alike to match. Work each one out: A rose 25% and B rose 20%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each rise as a percentage of its own original.

explain.text: A: $\tfrac{2}{8} = 0.25$. B: $\tfrac{20}{100} = 0.2$. The bigger pound rise was the smaller percentage rise.

feedback.correct: The £27.00 rise is one and a half times £18.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the rise by the original price.

byKey.ratio: 250% is the new price as a percentage of the old. Take away the 100% you started with.
byKey.new-base: You divided by £45.00, the new price. Divide the £27.00 rise by £18.00.
byKey.pounds: You wrote the £27.00 rise as a percentage. Divide it by £18.00 first.

explain.text: The rise is £27.00 and the original is £18.00: $\tfrac{27}{18} = 1.5$, a 150% rise. A rise can be more than 100%.
